source.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of The Richest Man in Babylon by George S. Clason (1926). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Public domain in the US since 2022, but in copyright until the end of 2027 in life+70 countries (the author died in 1957), so cards are original summaries without quotes.

cards.title: Keep a slice of everything you earn before you spend any of it
cards.body:
The book's central lesson, told through parables set in ancient Babylon, is that wealth starts when you treat part of every income as yours to keep. Clason's characters set aside at least one coin in ten before paying for anything else.

The point is the order. If saving waits until the bills and treats are covered, there is rarely anything left. Taken off the top, a tenth is small enough that you barely miss it, yet over years it grows into real security. Today that looks like an automatic transfer to savings on payday.
cards.apply_it: Set up an automatic transfer of 10% (or whatever you can start with) into a separate savings account on the day you are paid.

quiz.question: When does the book say you should set aside your savings?
options: After all bills are paid
Before spending anything else from your income
Only when you get a bonus
At the end of each year
quiz.explanation: Saving first, rather than saving what is left over, is what makes the habit stick.

cards.title: Spending rises to match income unless you separate needs from wants
cards.body:
Clason observes that what people call their necessary expenses tends to grow to fill whatever they earn. A pay rise rarely feels like more money for long, because new wants quietly become "needs".

His remedy is to look honestly at where money goes and sort it: what you genuinely require, and what you simply desire. Desires are endless, so you cannot satisfy them all; you choose the ones worth paying for and let the rest go. A simple budget makes those choices deliberate instead of accidental.
cards.apply_it: Go through last month's spending and mark each item as a need or a want. Pick one want to cut or reduce this month.

quiz.question: What does Clason say tends to happen to 'necessary expenses'?
options: They shrink as you get older
They stay fixed regardless of income
They grow to match whatever you earn
They are impossible to measure
quiz.explanation: Without a deliberate budget, wants creep in and expenses expand to swallow any income.

cards.title: Put your savings to work so they earn more money for you
cards.body:
Saved money sitting idle only protects you. Clason's wealthy characters go a step further: they lend or invest their savings so it produces its own income, and then they reinvest that income too.

The image is of money as a worker that brings back more workers. Each return adds to the pile that earns the next return, so growth speeds up over time. That is the idea of compounding, and it rewards starting early and leaving earnings to build rather than spending them as they arrive.
cards.apply_it: Check where your savings currently sit. If it earns little or nothing, research one low-cost, diversified option where it could grow over time.

quiz.question: Why does the book urge you to reinvest what your savings earn?
options: So that returns build on returns and growth speeds up
Because spending interest is illegal
To avoid paying any tax
Because idle money loses nothing
quiz.explanation: Reinvested earnings join the pile that produces the next round of earnings: compounding.

cards.title: Protect your savings by taking advice only from people who know the field
cards.body:
One of the book's warnings is that losing money is easier than making it. In a memorable parable, a man entrusts his savings to a brickmaker to buy jewels abroad, and the brickmaker is cheated with worthless glass. The lesson: why ask someone about a trade they have never practised?

Before committing money, Clason advises, make sure the principal is safe and seek counsel from people with real experience in that kind of investment. Tempting promises of fast, large returns deserve extra suspicion. Today this applies to tips from friends, social media hype and anything you do not understand.
cards.apply_it: Before your next financial decision, ask yourself: has the person advising me actually done this successfully, and could I afford to lose this money?

quiz.question: In the brickmaker parable, what went wrong?
options: The jewels were stolen on the road
He trusted someone with no experience in jewels, who was cheated
Interest rates suddenly rose
He invested too slowly
quiz.explanation: The saver asked for help from someone outside the trade; the lesson is to seek advice from people who know the field.

cards.title: Pay off debts with a fixed share of income while still saving
cards.body:
In one tale, a man deep in debt climbs out with a simple split of every earning: a small portion kept as savings, a larger portion divided among his creditors, and the rest to live on. He explains the plan to the people he owes, and pays each of them a little, regularly, until the debts are gone.

The wisdom still holds. Facing creditors honestly beats hiding from them, steady payments add up, and keeping some savings even while repaying stops you from sliding straight back into borrowing.
cards.apply_it: List every debt you have. Decide a fixed percentage of each payday that goes to repayments, and keep a small amount going to savings as well.

quiz.question: How did the indebted man in the story escape his debts?
options: By borrowing more to pay them off
By ignoring creditors until they gave up
By paying them a regular share of income while saving and living on the rest
By selling everything he owned at once
quiz.explanation: A fixed split between savings, repayments and living costs let him clear his debts steadily.

cards.title: Grow your earning power by getting better at your work
cards.body:
Saving and investing matter, but Clason also stresses the source of it all: your ability to earn. The more skill and knowledge you bring to your work, the more value you can offer, and the more you can reasonably ask to be paid.

His characters study their trades, learn from those ahead of them and take pride in doing work well. The modern version is treating your own skills as an investment: courses, practice, mentors and taking on harder responsibilities all compound into higher income over a career.
cards.apply_it: Name one skill that would make you noticeably more valuable at work. Block an hour this week to start learning it.

quiz.question: According to the book, what underlies all lasting wealth-building?
options: Luck and timing
A large inheritance
Increasing your own ability to earn
Avoiding all spending
quiz.explanation: Better skills raise the value you offer, which is the root of rising income.

cards.title: Plan now for the years when you can no longer earn
cards.body:
Clason points out that working life does not last forever, and that people who ignore this end up dependent on others. A wise person sets money aside so that income keeps coming in old age, and so their family is cared for if they die early.

He also suggests owning your home rather than paying rent forever, as a way to turn a regular cost into something of value. Today the same thinking points to pensions, retirement accounts and life insurance where it fits your situation.
cards.apply_it: Find out how much you are currently putting toward retirement. If it is nothing, set up even a small regular contribution this month.

quiz.question: Why does the book urge you to provide for the future?
options: Because earning years are limited and family may depend on you
Because money is worthless after 60
So you can stop saving today
Because renting is illegal
quiz.explanation: Income from work eventually stops, so preparing early protects you and those who depend on you.
